title: Testing and errors

stations.name: Why test a program?
facts: Testing finds bugs before users do. Other reasons: checking it meets the requirements, can't be misused, and has no security weak spots.
Real users type unexpected things and some try to break programs on purpose, so a robust program must cope with both.

questions.q: Which is a reason for testing a program before release?
questions.a: To find and fix errors so it works as intended

questions.q: Why should testers deliberately try to misuse a program?
questions.a: To check it won't crash or be exploited when users do something unexpected

stations.name: Iterative testing
facts: Iterative testing happens throughout development: each module is tested as it's written.
A fix in one place can have side effects elsewhere, so previously working parts are retested.

questions.q: When does iterative testing take place?
questions.a: While the program is being developed

questions.q: After fixing a bug in one module, why test the rest of the program again?
questions.a: To check the change hasn't broken code that already worked

stations.name: Final (terminal) testing
facts: Final testing happens once the program is complete, before release.
Iterative testing checks parts as they're built; final testing checks the whole program works together.

questions.a: Testing the complete program at the end of development, to check it meets all the requirements

questions.q: Which is most likely to be checked during final testing?
questions.a: Whether all the modules work together correctly

stations.name: Syntax errors
facts: Syntax is the grammar of a language. If the translator can't understand a line, the program won't run.
prnt is a misspelling of the keyword print, so Python doesn't recognise it.

questions.a: An error that breaks the rules of the programming language, so the code can't be translated or run

questions.q: Which line contains a syntax error?

stations.name: Logic errors
facts: Logic errors produce wrong results, loop forever or crash at the wrong moment, even though the code follows the rules.
You find logic errors by testing and checking the output against what you expected.

questions.a: The program runs, but doesn't do what the programmer intended

questions.q: Why are logic errors usually harder to find than syntax errors?
questions.a: The translator doesn't report them, because the code follows the language's rules

stations.name: Error detective
facts: Four errors: the wrong calculation, the missing items = items - 1, the misspelt print, and the missing int().
A misspelt keyword breaks the language's rules, so the code won't run.

questions.q: Which of these are errors in the total cost program? Select all that apply.
questions.a: total = total + total should be total = total + 3; Nothing inside the loop reduces items, so it never ends; prnt should be print; The input isn't converted to an integer before it is used

questions.q: Which type of error is prnt instead of print?

final.name: Final challenge: syntax or logic?

questions.q: Sort each bug: is it a syntax error or a logic error?
questions.a: prnt("2. Take register") = Syntax; choice = input(Enter choice:) with no quotation marks = Syntax; while items >= 1 with the colon missing = Syntax; valid = True before while not valid:, so the loop never runs = Logic; if not choice in [1,2,3]: when input() gives the string "2" = Logic; valid == True where valid = True was meant = Logic; average = total / count when count is 0 = Logic; Printing 'Fail' when the score is above the pass mark = Logic
